overview:
The state that would rule China for its last imperial stretch began outside it. In the forests northeast of the Great Wall, Nurhaci welded rival Jurchen clans into a single military society organized around the Eight Banners, and in 1616 declared a dynasty of his own. His son Hong Taiji renamed the people Manchu in 1635 and the state Great Qing in 1636 — a claim to universal rulership made before the group held a single Chinese province. The opening came in 1644, when the rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing and the Ming emperor hanged himself; the Ming general Wu Sangui opened the passes to the regent Dorgon rather than submit to the rebels. Beijing fell to the Manchus that summer, but the conquest was not a single event. Ming loyalist regimes in the south held out for nearly two decades, and Dorgon's queue order of 1645, which required Han men to shave their foreheads and braid their hair on pain of death, turned submission into a visible daily humiliation and provoked massacres in resisting cities.

What followed was one of the most successful long runs in Chinese history. The reigns of the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors spanned most of the period from 1661 to 1796 and are usually treated together as a high Qing age. Kangxi took Taiwan in 1683 and negotiated the Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia in 1689; Yongzheng tightened fiscal control and built channels, like the secret palace memorial, that let the throne hear from officials without the court filtering them; Qianlong's campaigns absorbed the Dzungar lands that became Xinjiang and confirmed Qing overlordship in Mongolia and Tibet. The empire that resulted was roughly the territorial shape modern China claims. It was governed in more than one register at once — as a Confucian dynasty running examinations and a merit bureaucracy for its Han subjects, and simultaneously as a Manchu house that spoke to Mongol allies as kin and to Tibetan Buddhists as patrons. Population tracked the peace, rising from perhaps a hundred million in the seventeenth century to some three hundred million by 1800 and around four hundred million by the end, a growth that pressed hard on land and helped feed later unrest.

The nineteenth century broke the arrangement from both directions. Britain's demand for a trade settlement it could impose ended in the Opium War of 1839–42 and a second war in 1856–60, producing treaty ports, extraterritoriality and indemnities. Internally the strain was far worse: the Taiping civil war of 1850–64 and the Muslim revolts in the northwest and southwest together killed tens of millions and left provincial armies, not the banners, holding the state together. Reform came in fits — the Self-Strengthening arsenals and shipyards after 1861, the Hundred Days of 1898 that Empress Dowager Cixi cut short, the sweeping late-Qing reforms after 1901 that abolished the examination system and introduced elected assemblies. Defeat by Japan in 1895 and the foreign occupation of Beijing after the Boxer Uprising in 1900 stripped away what prestige remained. When the Wuchang mutiny of October 1911 spread province by province, the court had few defenders left; the child emperor Puyi abdicated on 12 February 1912.
significance: The Qing assembled the territorial and demographic China that exists today — Xinjiang, Tibet, Mongolia and Manchuria were bound to the central provinces by Qing conquest and Qing diplomacy, and the borders and border disputes inherited by the Republic and then the People's Republic are largely Qing borders. It also produced the terms in which China's encounter with industrial imperialism is still argued about, from the unequal treaties to the question of whether the state failed to modernize or was prevented from doing so. And the dynasty's own nature remains genuinely unsettled: a generation of scholarship drawing on Manchu-language archives has argued that the Qing is better read as an Inner Asian empire that ruled China than as a Chinese dynasty that happened to have Manchu emperors — a reading with sharp present-day political stakes, since it recasts Qing expansion as conquest rather than reunification.
coverage: This dataset holds no mapped events for the Qing at all, so nothing above is drawn from it; the overview comes from general reference works and institutional summaries rather than from primary sources or specialist monographs. Even in the scholarly record, the picture is uneven — the conquest generation is known largely through Qing-authorized accounts that had reason to justify it, casualty figures for the Taiping and Dungan wars are estimates with enormous error bars, and the interpretation of Manchu rule itself is actively contested between the New Qing History school and Chinese scholars who read it as a sinicized Chinese dynasty. Nothing here should be taken as settled on that last point.
